title: Human Liver Anatomy: Lobes, Portal Vein & Biliary Tract
description: Study human liver anatomy, covering the four anatomical lobes, dual hepatic blood supply, porta hepatis, gallbladder, bile ducts, and metabolic lobule map.
h1: Human Liver Anatomy: Lobes, Portal Triad, Bile Ducts and Vessels
blurb: Fed by both the nutrient-rich portal vein and oxygen-rich hepatic artery, the liver's hexagonal lobules synthesize proteins, detoxify blood, and secrete bile.
lead: As the largest internal organ in the body, the liver sits beneath the right diaphragm and processes nearly every nutrient absorbed from the digestive tract. In this illustrated guide to human liver anatomy, we examine 20 documented structures—including right lobe, left lobe, caudate lobe, quadrate lobe—linking regional topography, tissue architecture, physiological mechanisms, and clinical reasoning.
overview: As the largest internal organ in the body, the liver sits beneath the right diaphragm and processes nearly every nutrient absorbed from the digestive tract. The liver receives blood twice over — oxygenated from the hepatic artery and nutrient-rich from the portal vein — and mixes them in the sinusoids between plates of hepatocytes. Each hepatocyte performs hundreds of jobs: making albumin and clotting factors, conjugating bilirubin, storing glycogen and vitamins, and detoxifying drugs through the cytochrome P450 system. Bile, made continuously, is concentrated in the gallbladder and released into the duodenum to emulsify fat. The liver is also the only visceral organ that can regenerate: removing 70% leaves a liver that regrows to full size. Within the human body, the liver (Hepar) is situated in right hypochondrium & epigastrium, under the diaphragm, receives arterial perfusion via dual: hepatic artery (25%) + hepatic portal vein (75%), and is innervated by hepatic plexus (vagus + sympathetic coeliac fibres).

The right lobe (Lobus dexter) is the larger lobe, four to six times the volume of the left, occupying the right hypochondrium. Its diaphragmatic surface is smooth and convex. Physiologically, the right lobe carries most of the hepatic mass and function. Structurally, the left lobe (Lobus sinister) comprises thinner and flatter, lying in the epigastrium and reaching across to the left. Separated from the right lobe on the diaphragmatic surface by the falciform ligament. Physiologically, the left lobe supplies the left half of the functional liver. The caudate lobe (Lobus caudatus) is a small lobe on the posterior surface between the IVC and the ligamentum venosum, draining directly into the IVC. Physiologically, the caudate lobe governs has independent vascular supply and biliary drainage. Anatomically, the quadrate lobe (Lobus quadratus) lies on the visceral surface between the gallbladder fossa and the fissure for the ligamentum teres. Physiologically, the quadrate lobe governs functionally part of the left hemiliver. The falciform ligament (Ligamentum falciforme) is a sickle-shaped fold of peritoneum attaching the liver to the anterior abdominal wall and diaphragm; its free edge carries the ligamentum teres (obliterated umbilical vein). Physiologically, the falciform ligament anchors the liver and divides the anatomical lobes on the diaphragmatic surface. The gallbladder (Vesica biliaris) is a 7–10 cm pear-shaped sac on the visceral surface of the right lobe, with fundus, body and neck. Its wall concentrates bile up to tenfold. Physiologically, the gallbladder stores and concentrates bile, releasing it into the duodenum when fat arrives (CCK-mediated).

Clinically, regarding the right lobe, its inferior edge is what you palpate below the costal margin in hepatomegaly. From a diagnostic standpoint, in the left lobe, in cirrhosis the left and caudate lobes often hypertrophy while the right lobe atrophies. In clinical pathology involving the caudate lobe, it hypertrophies in Budd–Chiari syndrome, and its size relative to the right lobe is a CT sign of cirrhosis. Medical evaluation of the quadrate lobe also notes that together with the caudate lobe it defines the surgical anatomy of the portohepatic segments.

questions.question: What are the main functions of the liver?
questions.answer: The liver processes nutrients, makes bile and many blood proteins, stores glycogen and participates in drug and toxin metabolism. Its blood arrives from both the portal vein and hepatic artery. Structurally, the hepatic lobule & sinusoids (Lobulus hepaticus) comprises hexagonal units ~1 mm across: plates of hepatocytes radiating from a central vein, separated by sinusoids lined with endothelium and Kupffer macrophages; portal triads (artery, vein, bile duct) sit at the corners. Physiologically, the hepatic lobule & sinusoids governs blood flows from triad to central vein while bile flows the opposite way, from canaliculi to the triad bile duct.

questions.question: Where is the liver located?
questions.answer: Most of the liver lies beneath the diaphragm in the right upper abdomen, with a smaller part extending across the midline. Structurally, the left lobe (Lobus sinister) comprises thinner and flatter, lying in the epigastrium and reaching across to the left. Separated from the right lobe on the diaphragmatic surface by the falciform ligament. Physiologically, the left lobe supplies the left half of the functional liver.

questions.question: What is the gallbladder?
questions.answer: A 7–10 cm pear-shaped sac on the visceral surface of the right lobe, with fundus, body and neck. Its wall concentrates bile up to tenfold. Functionally, it stores and concentrates bile, releasing it into the duodenum when fat arrives (CCK-mediated). In clinical pathology involving the gallbladder, gallstones (cholelithiasis) cause biliary colic; a stone impacted in the neck gives acute cholecystitis with Murphy's sign.

questions.question: Where is the hepatic portal vein located?
questions.answer: Formed behind the pancreatic neck by the splenic and superior mesenteric veins; carries nutrient-rich, deoxygenated blood from gut, spleen and pancreas. Functionally, it delivers 75% of hepatic blood and everything absorbed from the gut for first-pass processing. Medical evaluation of the hepatic portal vein also notes that portal hypertension (cirrhosis) causes oesophageal varices, splenomegaly and ascites.

questions.question: What is the function of the hepatic lobule & sinusoids?
questions.answer: Functionally, it governs blood flows from triad to central vein while bile flows the opposite way, from canaliculi to the triad bile duct. Hexagonal units ~1 mm across: plates of hepatocytes radiating from a central vein, separated by sinusoids lined with endothelium and Kupffer macrophages; portal triads (artery, vein, bile duct) sit at the corners. Structurally, the hepatic sinusoid (Sinusoideum hepaticum) comprises wide, discontinuous capillary channel between plates of hepatocytes. Physiologically, the hepatic sinusoid allows blood–hepatocyte exchange en route to central vein.
